notes.body:
The answer is simpler than the two names make it seem: **'the Imam' and Maulana Ali are one and the same person.** Throughout the chapter the author describes a single figure — the first Imam — and only moves between two ways of naming him.

When a saying is introduced with the honorific, the text writes "Ali (ع)"; when the author is thinking of him in his office — his rank and function as guide of the community — he calls him "the Imam." Both point to the same voice behind the sermons, the supplications such as دعاء كميل, and the hadith of حقيقة.

One detail seals it. The disciple who asks the Imam about حقيقة is Kumayl, and Kumayl was Maulana Ali's own companion. So the sermon on the greatness of the Quran, the supplication of the lame man, and the saying that *he who loves a thing dedicates himself fervently to its invocation* all rise from one heart.

How, then, does a reader tell one imam from another? By a single rule the author keeps faithfully:

- "The Imam," standing alone with no name attached, always means Maulana Ali.
- Any other imam is named in full — Imam Jafar al-Sadiq, or his father Imam Muhammad al-Baqir.
- "Ali (ع)" and "the Imam" never name two different people; they are one person seen from two angles.

Watch this in action. When the text says al-Baqir "never ceased invoking, even while eating and walking," that later imam is named on purpose — precisely so he is not mistaken for the Imam of the chapter. The naming itself is the whole signal: **an unnamed Imam is Maulana Ali, and a named one is only ever himself.**

etymology: إمام (leader, guide): from the root أ-م-م, carrying the sense of intending something and heading out in front of it. The same root yields أمام, meaning 'in front,' and أُمّ, 'mother' or source. An إمام is the one set ahead, whom a community faces and follows — the pattern others align themselves to.

ذِكْر (remembrance): the verbal noun of ذَكَرَ, 'he remembered, he mentioned,' from the root ذ-ك-ر. The root spans inward memory, spoken mention, and reminder all at once, so a single word holds both the silent recollection of the heart and its utterance on the tongue.

تَوَحُّد (self-integration): a reflexive form built on the root و-ح-د, 'to be one.' Where تَوْحِيد declares that Allah is One, تَوَحُّد turns the same root inward — the soul gathering its scattered parts into one undivided orientation.

notes.body:
These two sentences belong to one and the same saying. What is quoted here — "until I love him" — is only the opening of a longer hadith qudsi (حديث قدسي), a report in which Allah speaks in the first person through the tongue of the Prophet. The author pauses at the moment of love to dwell on it, but the divine speech does not stop there.

In its complete form the hadith runs on without a break:

فَإِذَا أَحْبَبْتُهُ كُنْتُ سَمْعَهُ الَّذِي يَسْمَعُ بِهِ وَبَصَرَهُ الَّذِي يُبْصِرُ بِهِ وَيَدَهُ الَّتِي يَبْطِشُ بِهَا وَرِجْلَهُ الَّتِي يَمْشِي بِهَا

"And when I love him, I become the hearing by which he hears, the sight by which he sees, the hand by which he grasps, and the foot by which he walks."

So "the hearing and the seeing" is not a separate report stitched on afterwards — it is **the very next clause of the same hadith**.

This report is well known and carries its own name: it is often called the hadith of nearness, and its subject is the supererogatory acts, the نوافل. Picture it as a single sentence spoken to us in two halves:

1. The first half names the road — drawing near through freely offered devotion until love is won.
2. The second half names the destination — Allah becoming the very faculties through which the beloved lives.

Quoting only the first half is like citing "I have loved you" and letting the promise that follows stay understood.

Why does the passage break off where it does? Because its whole argument is about agency — about who truly acts, who truly hears and sees. The author withholds the second half for a few sentences so that, when it finally arrives, we feel its weight: our devotions were ours only in appearance, but **the seeing was His all along**. It is the same mystery held in the promise,

"Remember Me, I will remember you."
Al-Baqarah 2:152
notes.anchor: God is the hearing and the seeing of the individual whom He loves
notes.quote: God is the hearing and the seeing of the individual whom He loves
etymology: نوافل (supererogatory acts): from the root ن-ف-ل, carrying the sense of a surplus or an extra gift given beyond what is owed. A نافلة is worship offered over and above the obligatory, freely and out of love — which is precisely why it is the thing that draws a servant nearer.

قرب (nearness): from the root ق-ر-ب, to come close. The reflexive verb يتقرب means to keep actively seeking closeness, step after step; the same root yields قربان, an offering whose purpose is to close the distance between a servant and Allah.

notes.body:
Everything here turns on one small verb, تكن, and on the silence a reader places after it. Not a single letter is added, removed, or re-shaped between the two readings — the consonants stay exactly as they were. What moves is **where the voice comes to rest**, and that alone reassigns the work each word is doing.

Read straight through, تكن is a helper that leans forward onto the verb after it.
إن لم تكن تراه
"and if you see Him not"
On its own تكن means only "you are" — an unfinished word waiting for its completion — and it reaches ahead to take تراه, "you see Him," as that completion. The two fuse into a single thought, "you are not seeing Him," and the negation لم spreads across the whole of it. **The seeing is swallowed inside the denial.**

Now let a pause fall after تكن, and the helper is cut loose from what follows. Standing alone, تكن no longer means "you are something"; it means "you exist." The three roles laid bare:

- Without the pause, تكن leans on تراه and the negation covers both together: "you do not see Him."
- With the pause, تكن stands by itself as "you exist," so the negation reaches only that far: "you are not."
- Freed from تكن, the verb تراه is left with nothing to negate it and turns positive: "you see Him."

So the second reading is not a different set of words but the same words differently governed:
إن لم تكن، تراه
"if you are not, you see Him." Once the negation can no longer reach تراه, the vision stands affirmed. **It is our own being, not the letters, that the pause takes away** — and in that removal the seeing of Him becomes possible, for the eye that beholds Him is no longer clouded by the one who was looking.

etymology: كان: from the root ك-و-ن, "to come to be." It lives two lives in one word — as a leaning helper it means merely "to be something," but standing alone it means "to exist," the same root that yields كون, the whole created order. The second reading simply lets the word live its stronger, existential life.

رأى: from the root ر-أ-ي, "to see," and beyond the physical eye "to perceive" and "to hold as true." From it comes رؤية, a beholding or vision — the very sight the saying promises will open once the self has fallen away.

وقف: from the root و-ق-ف, "to stand, to halt." The reciter's pause is a deliberate standing-still of the voice. Here that halt is not decoration but the hinge itself, freeing one verb from the next so each recovers a meaning it could not carry while they were joined.

notes.body:
*Researched outside this library — the knowledge base carries nothing on this passage. Sources are listed at the end.*

To understand the ‘immutable entity’ (الأعيان الثابتة), we must first see it not as a *thing* in our world, but as a reality in the knowledge of Allah. These are the eternal, uncreated essences of every possible being, existing forever within Allah’s awareness before they are ever brought into the world of form and time. They are described as ‘inexistent in themselves’ because they do not possess external, physical existence; you cannot touch or see them. Yet, they are profoundly real, for they are eternally known by Allah.

Imagine an architect who holds the complete and perfect blueprint of a house in his mind. That blueprint is not the house itself; you cannot take shelter in the idea. In this sense, the blueprint is ‘inexistent’ as a physical structure. However, this very blueprint dictates the entire reality of the house that will be built—its shape, its size, its every detail. It is the unchangeable pattern that determines the final form.

In the same way, the **immutable entity** is the unique, spiritual blueprint for each one of us. When Allah wills a being into existence, He does not create it from nothing in that moment. Rather, He bestows the gift of existence upon its eternal reality, causing a reflection or manifestation of that blueprint to appear in the created world. The entity itself remains fixed and unchanging in His knowledge, acting as the permanent, receptive mold that gives the created being its specific contours, form, and destiny. Thus, the ‘inexistent’ idea becomes the absolute determinant of the ‘existent’ being.

***

عين (entity): From the root ع-ي-ن, which carries primary meanings of ‘eye’ and ‘spring’ or ‘source.’ As ‘eye,’ it signifies perception and individuality. As ‘source,’ it points to an origin. In this context, عين refers to the very essence, the unique identity, and the spiritual source of a specific being as it is known by Allah.

ثابتة (immutable): From the root ث-ب-ت, meaning to be firm, fixed, proven, or established. The word ثابتة conveys a state of permanence and unchangeability. It emphasizes that these essential realities are eternally established in Allah’s knowledge and do not alter when they are manifested in creation.

**Sources consulted**

- ijicc.net
- ibnarabisociety.org
- iqraonline.net
- academia.edu

notes.body:
The word points back to a single teacher. Akbari comes from a title of deep honour, الشيخ الأكبر — "the Greatest Master" — which later generations gave to Muhyi al-Din Ibn al-Arabi, the Andalusian sage who lived some six centuries after Maulana Ali. To call a teaching **Akbari**, then, is simply to say it belongs to his school, the wide current of thought that flowed out from his writings.

That school is one of the great streams within Sufi contemplation, and this passage sets Maulana Ali's own teaching on the ultimate Reality (الحقيقة) at its very spring. The gentle claim being made is that what Ibn al-Arabi later unfolds across thousands of pages already lies folded, **like a seed**, inside the Imam's few luminous sentences to his disciple Kumayl.

At the heart of that school is one idea: the **self-disclosure** (تجلي) of the Hidden — the moment the unseen Reality shines out where it can be seen. The doctrine holds that the single Light of Allah pours upon countless receptacles, and each one receives that one Light in its own measure and its own colour. Three familiar images carry the meaning:

- light passing through stained glass, one radiance breaking into many hues;
- water taking on the colour of whatever cup it fills;
- a mirror, which shows the sun only once its rust is wiped away.

Every soul is such a vessel — a مظهر, a place where the one Light appears — and this is why the same tradition treasures the polishing of the heart through remembrance. The Light itself never alters; **what changes is the cup**. Our whole task is to become glass clear enough that the one radiance passes through us undistorted, so that what shines in us is not our own colour but His.

etymology: أكبر (greatest): from the root ك-ب-ر, carrying the sense of being great or growing large. It is the superlative form, lifting mere 'great' to 'greatest' — the honour behind the title الشيخ الأكبر given to Ibn al-Arabi.

تجلي (self-disclosure): from the root ج-ل-و, meaning to become clear, to unveil, even to polish until a thing shines. The word names the very moment a hidden Reality shows itself — clarity breaking out of concealment.

مظهر (locus of manifestation): from the root ظ-ه-ر, to appear, to become outward and visible. A مظهر is the place where something shows itself — here, the vessel or soul in which the one Light of Allah becomes visible.

notes.body:
What looks like a contradiction dissolves once we notice WHAT is being deepened. The remembrance (ذِكْر) does not swell the self's awareness of itself; it deepens awareness of the Real, and these two grow in opposite directions. **The more vividly the heart perceives Allah, the less it perceives itself as a separate doer** — not because consciousness dims, but because it has finally turned all the way toward its source.

Think of a window being polished. While the glass is smudged, we keep noticing the glass; once it is perfectly clean, we see only the light streaming through. The invocation is that polishing, and the fading of the self is the sign that the heart has become fully transparent. The extinction (فَنَاء) is not a loss of awareness but its completion.

At its height, remembrance reveals a truth that was always so: the one truly invoking is not us. Maulana Ali teaches that invocation comes forth firstly from the Invoked (اَلْمَذْكُور), and only secondly from the invoker (اَلذَّاكِر). Our remembering was ever the shadow of Allah's remembering of us, which is why the verse can be read as a promise that begins on His side:

فَٱذْكُرُونِىٓ أَذْكُرْكُمْ
"Remember Me, I will remember you."
Al-Baqarah 2:152

So the path of deepening consciousness runs through three stages:

1. remembrance polishes the heart and clears away heedlessness (غَفْلَة);
2. the cleared heart sees the Real (اَلْحَقّ) ever more directly;
3. seeing so directly, it sees THROUGH its own false separateness, and the center of awareness passes from the self to Allah.

This is why **the fullest waking is also the deepest self-forgetting**. The little flame is not blown out; it is out-shone, gathered up into a light so total that nothing stands beside it — and there, as the Imam says, there is no difference between the lover and the Beloved.
notes.anchor: why and how does the dhikr bring about this extinction of consciousness
notes.quote: why and how does the dhikr bring about this extinction of consciousness
etymology: ذِكْر (remembrance): from the root ذ-ك-ر, meaning both to mention aloud and to hold in mind. The same root yields اَلذَّاكِر, the one who invokes, and اَلْمَذْكُور, the One invoked, so the very word binds speaking and remembering, invoker and Invoked, into a single act.

فَنَاء (extinction): from the root ف-ن-ي, to pass away, to be spent, to come to an end. It is not annihilation into nothing but the passing-away of the self's separate standing, the way a shadow is spent the moment the full light arrives.

غَفْلَة (heedlessness): from the root غ-ف-ل, to be inattentive, to let a thing slip from notice. It names not active denial but a drifting forgetfulness — the film of neglect that settles over the heart and that remembrance is meant to wipe clean.
